feedback: If a learner writes 4 + 3 + 5 = 12, return to one layer of 4 × 3 and five layers: adding gives an edge total, not a cube count — all three dimensions must be multiplied.
If a learner computes 4 × 3 = 12 and stops, ask how many layers tall the box is; the height is still needed.

If the answer is written as 60 cm², link cm³ to a single filling unit cube and distinguish filling a space (volume, cm³) from covering faces (surface area, cm²); the multiplication itself may be correct.
For a missing-edge task, check the learner divides the volume by the product of the two known edges rather than guessing.
activities.intendedInsight: The formula is a tool for real problems: you can run it forwards (edges to volume), backwards (volume and two edges to the third), and in the B × h form, and you must use all three dimensions and the cubic unit.
learnerActions: Compute the volume of several labelled cuboids using V = l × w × h, writing the unit as cm³ each time.
Find a missing edge length when given a prism's volume and two of its dimensions.
Given the base area B and height h (instead of three separate edges), compute V = B × h.
Compare two cuboids and decide which holds more, estimating before calculating.
Spot and correct worked examples that add the dimensions (l + w + h) or multiply only two of the three.
activities.title: Apply and compare prism volumes
